title: Gulab Jamun
subtitle: milk solid dumplings in rose syrup
excerpt: Gulab jamun are soft, spongy milk-based dumplings deep-fried until golden and soaked in a fragrant rose-water and cardamom syrup. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Gulab jamun evolved from a Persian dish called luqmat al-qadi brought to India by Mughal court cooks, made here with dried milk powder as an accessible substitute for khoya.

recipe.batchNotes: Makes 16 dumplings. Double the recipe for a larger batch. They keep in syrup in the fridge for 5 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make a day ahead. The dumplings absorb more syrup as they sit and become softer.
recipe.temperatureNote: Low frying temperature is critical. Too hot and the outside browns before the centre cooks.

glossaryTerms.definition: Deep-fried milk-solid dumplings soaked in sugar syrup flavoured with rose water and cardamom. Gulab means rose; jamun refers to a dark berry the dumplings resemble.
A simple sugar syrup flavoured with rose water and cardamom, used to soak gulab jamun until they become spongy.

content.text: while still warm. The syrup must be warm too. If either is cold, the dumplings harden rather than absorbing the liquid.
Fry at 150 C, not higher. The dumplings take 8 to 10 minutes to cook through. Patience here prevents a raw centre.

Make the syrup first: dissolve sugar in 400 ml water over low heat. Add half the cardamom and lemon juice. Simmer 5 minutes until slightly syrupy. Remove from heat and stir in rose water if using. Keep warm.
If reducing milk to make khoya: simmer whole milk in a non-stick pan over medium heat, stirring continuously, for 20 to 25 minutes until it reduces to a thick, dough-like mass. Cool completely.
Mix the cooled khoya (or 150g full-fat milk powder) with plain flour, softened butter, remaining cardamom, and just enough milk to bring together into a smooth, soft dough. Do not overwork.
Rest the dough 20 minutes. Divide into 16 equal pieces. Roll each into a smooth ball with no cracks.
Heat oil to 150 C. Fry dumplings in small batches of 4 to 5, rolling gently in the oil, for 8 to 10 minutes until evenly dark golden brown.
Remove with a slotted spoon. Immediately place into the warm syrup. Leave to soak for at least 30 minutes. They will swell and become spongy.
Serve warm with a scoop of ice cream or a spoonful of the syrup. Scatter pistachios on top.

attrs.symptom: Dumplings are dark on the outside but raw in the centre
attrs.fix: Reduce oil temperature to 150 C. Fry more slowly. The dumplings should take a full 8 to 10 minutes to colour.

attrs.symptom: Dumplings do not absorb the syrup
attrs.cause: Either the syrup or the dumplings were too cold when combined
attrs.fix: Warm both the syrup and the dumplings gently before combining. Pierce each dumpling once with a skewer to help absorption.

attrs.symptom: Dumplings break apart in the oil
attrs.cause: Dough was too dry or not rested
attrs.fix: Add a teaspoon of milk to the dough and knead gently. Rest for a further 10 minutes before rolling.

content.text: Gulab jamun is one of the most widely eaten sweets across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and the Indian diaspora worldwide. The name comes from the Persian and Arabic: gulab means rose water and jamun is a dark berry of similar size and shape. The sweet arrived in India with Mughal cooks who adapted Persian luqaimat. The modern version made with milk powder was popularised when khoya became harder to source commercially. It is served at virtually every wedding, festival, and celebration.
